questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which statement best describes adult medical-surgical nursing?

options.text: It addresses acute illness, chronic disease, injury and surgery while considering the whole person.
It focuses only on the disease diagnosis.
It is limited to postoperative care.
It excludes psychological and social needs.

questions.rationale: Adult medical-surgical nursing considers physical, psychological, social, cultural and functional needs in addition to the medical diagnosis.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: What is the FIRST stage of the nursing process?
questions.rationale: Assessment gathers the information needed to identify problems and plan care.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which stage of the nursing process determines whether the care plan is working?
questions.rationale: Evaluation compares outcomes with goals and identifies whether the plan should continue or change.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has low oxygen saturation and weakness. Which problem should the nurse address FIRST?
questions.rationale: Airway and breathing take priority over less urgent problems.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Why is pathophysiology important in nursing care?

options.text: It helps the nurse interpret symptoms and anticipate complications.
It is relevant only to doctors.
It removes the need for monitoring.

questions.rationale: Understanding altered body function helps nurses connect symptoms with disease processes and recognise risks.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure develops breathlessness and ankle swelling. What underlying process is most likely contributing?
questions.rationale: Heart failure can lead to fluid retention, pulmonary congestion and peripheral oedema.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects person-centred care?

options.text: Use the same plan for every patient.
Consider how illness affects the person's comfort, function, family and goals.
Delay discussion of social needs until discharge.

questions.rationale: Person-centred care addresses the individual's physical, emotional, social and functional needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient with severe postoperative pain avoids coughing. What complication may this increase?
questions.rationale: Pain can limit deep breathing and coughing, increasing the risk of atelectasis and pneumonia.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which finding should be considered most urgent?

options.text: Chronic knee pain unchanged for months.

questions.rationale: New breathing difficulty may be life-threatening and requires immediate assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: The nursing process is best described as:

options.text: A continuous cycle of assessment, planning, action and evaluation.
A task completed only on admission.
A process used only for complex patients.

questions.rationale: The nursing process is continuous and changes as the patient's condition and needs change.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes has a slow-healing wound. Which relationship is most important?

options.text: Wounds are unrelated to glucose control.
Diabetes may impair healing and increase infection risk.

questions.rationale: Poor glucose control may impair circulation, immune function and wound healing.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse identifies several patient problems. Which should be prioritised FIRST?
questions.rationale: Potentially life-threatening circulation problems take priority.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient has infection, confusion and low blood pressure. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Infection with confusion and hypotension may indicate serious deterioration and requires urgent escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which factor may influence an adult patient's response to illness?

options.text: Culture, function, family support and previous health.

questions.rationale: Responses to illness are shaped by physical, psychological, social and cultural factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient says financial concerns may prevent purchasing prescribed medicines. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore the concern because it is non-clinical.
Tell the patient to manage independently.
Include the concern in care planning and seek appropriate support.

questions.rationale: Financial circumstances can affect treatment adherence and recovery and should be addressed through care planning and referral.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which goal is most measurable?

options.text: The patient will feel better soon.
The patient will walk 20 metres with assistance by the end of the shift.

questions.rationale: Measurable goals specify the expected outcome, conditions and timeframe.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse completes an intervention but does not reassess the patient. Which nursing-process stage is missing?
questions.rationale: Evaluation is required to determine the patient's response and whether care was effective.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient with COPD reports worsening breathlessness but normal temperature. What is the BEST interpretation?

options.text: Absence of fever means the patient is stable.
Breathing changes require assessment regardless of temperature.

questions.rationale: Clinical reasoning considers the whole picture; worsening breathlessness may signal deterioration even without fever.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: What best demonstrates prioritisation in adult nursing?

options.text: Completing tasks in the order written.
Responding first to the loudest patient.
Addressing airway, breathing, circulation and immediate safety before routine care.

questions.rationale: Priority care is based on urgency, instability and risk, not task order or convenience.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects effective adult medical-surgical nursing?

options.text: The same care plan is used for all patients.
The patient receives coordinated, individualised care that improves safety and function.

questions.rationale: Effective care integrates assessment, prioritisation, intervention, evaluation and person-centred goals.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Why is establishing a patient's baseline important?

options.text: It helps identify new or worsening changes.
It is needed only for discharge.

questions.rationale: Knowing the patient's usual condition makes subtle deterioration easier to recognise.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which assessment approach is most appropriate for an adult patient?

options.text: Assessment of the painful area only.

questions.rationale: A systematic assessment reduces omissions and provides a complete clinical picture.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A patient's respiratory rate rises from 18 to 30 breaths per minute. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore it if blood pressure is normal.
Recognise this as a possible early sign of deterioration and assess promptly.

questions.rationale: A rising respiratory rate is an important early warning sign and requires prompt assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which combination is most concerning after surgery?

options.text: Stable blood pressure, normal urine output and mild pain.
Rising respiratory rate, reduced urine output and restlessness.

questions.rationale: The combination suggests possible early deterioration despite a normal blood pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which assessment finding requires urgent escalation?
questions.rationale: Acute change in consciousness may indicate serious neurological, respiratory or circulatory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A nurse documents 'patient looks unwell.' What additional information is needed?

options.text: Objective observations and specific assessment findings.

questions.rationale: Documentation should be objective, measurable and clinically meaningful.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which result is most relevant when assessing renal function?
questions.rationale: Renal function is commonly assessed using creatinine, urine output and related laboratory values.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A patient's blood glucose is low and the patient is sweaty and confused. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Sweating and confusion are common signs of hypoglycaemia.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which finding may suggest poor tissue perfusion?

options.text: Cool skin, confusion and reduced urine output.
Warm dry skin and normal cognition.
Stable pulse and good urine output.

questions.rationale: Cool skin, altered cognition and reduced urine output can indicate impaired circulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A single blood pressure reading is normal, but the patient's condition appears worse. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the complete clinical picture and observation trends.

questions.rationale: One normal value does not exclude deterioration; trends and other cues must be considered.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which statement best describes clinical reasoning?

options.text: Collecting cues, interpreting their meaning and deciding appropriate action.
Waiting for medical instructions before assessment.

questions.rationale: Clinical reasoning integrates assessment findings, baseline and context to guide decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Why should a nurse assess medication history during admission?

options.text: It is relevant only to pharmacy.
It is needed only before discharge.
It does not affect clinical reasoning.
Medicines may affect symptoms, risks and current treatment.

questions.rationale: Medication history may explain symptoms, interactions and treatment needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A patient has reduced urine output after surgery. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Assess fluid balance, observations and possible causes, then escalate if indicated.
Encourage large fluid intake without assessment.

questions.rationale: Reduced urine output may indicate hypovolaemia, renal impairment or deterioration and requires assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which finding is most important when assessing respiratory function?

options.text: Work of breathing and oxygen saturation.

questions.rationale: Respiratory effort, rate, breath sounds and oxygen saturation are key findings.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A patient has increasing abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Increasing pain with rigidity may indicate an acute abdominal emergency.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which assessment best evaluates fluid balance?

options.text: Intake, output, daily weight, oedema and blood pressure.

questions.rationale: Multiple indicators are needed to evaluate fluid status accurately.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Why are trends more useful than isolated observations?

options.text: They show direction and progression of change over time.
They eliminate the need for assessment.
They apply only to intensive care.

questions.rationale: Trends may reveal deterioration before one value becomes severely abnormal.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: A family member says the patient is 'not acting normally.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Dismiss it without abnormal vital signs.
Take the concern seriously and reassess the patient.
Tell them to wait for the doctor.

questions.rationale: Families may detect subtle changes early and their concerns should prompt assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which result may indicate infection?

options.text: Raised white blood cell count with fever and clinical symptoms.

questions.rationale: An elevated white blood cell count, fever and clinical signs may support infection.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment and Clinical Reasoning
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective clinical reasoning?

options.text: The nurse completes the observation chart.
The nurse waits for one severely abnormal value.
The nurse documents only the diagnosis.
The nurse recognises subtle deterioration, reassesses and escalates before severe harm.

questions.rationale: Effective reasoning links cues and trends to timely action.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure gains 2 kg in three days. What is the most likely concern?
questions.rationale: Rapid weight gain in heart failure commonly indicates fluid accumulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding requires urgent review in a patient with coronary artery disease?
questions.rationale: New chest pain may indicate acute myocardial ischaemia and requires urgent assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with COPD becomes increasingly drowsy and fatigued while breathing. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Increasing fatigue and drowsiness may indicate worsening respiratory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which intervention commonly supports a breathless patient?

options.text: Positioning upright and completing respiratory assessment.

questions.rationale: Upright positioning can improve ventilation while the nurse assesses severity and treatment needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has thick sputum. Which intervention may support secretion clearance?

options.text: Hydration as appropriate and prescribed respiratory care.

questions.rationale: Appropriate hydration, positioning, coughing and prescribed treatment may help mobilise secretions.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with fluid overload?
questions.rationale: Fluid overload commonly causes oedema, pulmonary congestion and increased weight.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with kidney impairment is prescribed several medicines. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: Kidney function does not affect medicines.
Reduced medication clearance and risk of accumulation.

questions.rationale: Renal impairment may reduce elimination and increase toxicity risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which assessment is most important for a patient with vomiting?

options.text: Hydration status, electrolytes and fluid balance.

questions.rationale: Vomiting can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A diabetic patient becomes shaky, sweaty and confused. What is the priority?

options.text: Assess and treat possible hypoglycaemia according to protocol.

questions.rationale: These are classic symptoms of low blood glucose requiring prompt treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which patient teaching is most important for heart failure self-management?

options.text: Daily weight monitoring and reporting rapid gains.

questions.rationale: Daily weights help detect fluid retention early.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with asthma has difficulty speaking and severe breathlessness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the patient to rest quietly.
Treat as urgent deterioration and escalate immediately.

questions.rationale: Severe breathlessness and inability to speak normally may indicate a life-threatening asthma exacerbation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding?
questions.rationale: Melaena and dizziness may indicate significant gastrointestinal blood loss.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with renal impairment develops muscle weakness and an abnormal potassium level. Why is this concerning?

options.text: Electrolyte imbalance may affect cardiac function.
It is unrelated to renal disease.

questions.rationale: Potassium abnormalities can cause dangerous arrhythmias and weakness.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which intervention best supports diabetic foot care?

options.text: Regular inspection, appropriate footwear and prompt reporting of injury.
Applying heat directly to numb feet.

questions.rationale: Reduced sensation and healing increase risk; prevention and early reporting are essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with COPD is prescribed oxygen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop oxygen when the patient sleeps.
Administer as prescribed and monitor respiratory response.
Rely only on the device setting.

questions.rationale: Oxygen therapy requires prescribed administration and ongoing assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure becomes hypotensive after treatment. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Hypotension may indicate reduced perfusion or treatment-related complications.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which measure is useful for evaluating kidney-related fluid status?
questions.rationale: Weight and fluid balance are key indicators of fluid retention or loss.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes has a worsening wound. What should the nurse assess?

options.text: Blood glucose control, infection signs and circulation.

questions.rationale: Diabetes can impair healing; glucose, infection and perfusion should be assessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which action best supports self-management of chronic illness?

options.text: Teaching warning signs and when to seek help.

questions.rationale: Patients need practical education about monitoring, treatment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Nursing Care for Common Medical Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects effective care for common medical conditions?

options.text: The nurse monitors disease and treatment effects, prevents complications and supports self-management.

questions.rationale: Effective medical nursing combines monitoring, intervention, complication prevention and education.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which preoperative check is essential before surgery?

options.text: Correct patient identity, consent process, allergies and fasting status.

questions.rationale: Preoperative safety requires confirmation of identity, consent, allergies, fasting and preparation requirements.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: What is the first priority immediately after surgery?
questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are immediate postoperative priorities.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which finding may indicate postoperative bleeding?

options.text: Tachycardia, falling blood pressure and increasing wound drainage.

questions.rationale: Changes in circulation and wound drainage may indicate haemorrhage.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Why is pain control important after surgery?

options.text: It is needed only for comfort.
It supports breathing, coughing, movement and rest.

questions.rationale: Effective pain relief promotes respiratory function, mobility and recovery.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which intervention helps prevent postoperative respiratory complications?

options.text: Deep breathing, coughing and early mobilisation.

questions.rationale: Breathing exercises and mobilisation reduce atelectasis and pneumonia risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: A patient develops calf pain and swelling after knee surgery. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Unilateral calf pain and swelling after surgery may indicate deep vein thrombosis.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: What should the nurse do if venous thromboembolism is suspected?

options.text: Stop unnecessary mobilisation, assess and escalate urgently.

questions.rationale: Massage or mobilisation may be unsafe; urgent assessment and escalation are required.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which intervention reduces pressure-injury risk after surgery?

options.text: Leaving the patient in one position.

questions.rationale: Repositioning, skin care and pressure redistribution reduce injury risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: A patient has increasing wound redness, pain and fever. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Assess for infection and escalate promptly.

questions.rationale: These findings may indicate surgical-site infection and require review.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Why should postoperative urine output be monitored?

options.text: It helps assess perfusion, hydration and renal function.
It is needed only after kidney surgery.

questions.rationale: Reduced urine output may indicate hypovolaemia, renal impairment or deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which action supports prevention of venous thromboembolism?
questions.rationale: Mobilisation and prescribed mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis reduce risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: A postoperative patient becomes restless with rising respiratory rate. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess immediately and escalate possible deterioration.

questions.rationale: Restlessness and tachypnoea may be early signs of hypoxia or other complications.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which finding should be included in immediate postoperative assessment?

options.text: Consciousness, pain, wound, drains and circulation.

questions.rationale: Immediate assessment includes neurological status, circulation, pain, wound and devices.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: A patient refuses deep-breathing exercises because of pain. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review pain control, explain the purpose and support the exercises.

questions.rationale: Pain management and education can enable participation in complication prevention.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: What is the best indicator that postoperative pain management is effective?

options.text: The pain score is never assessed.
The patient can breathe deeply, move and rest with tolerable pain.

questions.rationale: Effectiveness is shown by improved function and comfort after treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Why should discharge planning begin early?

options.text: It is needed only for older adults.
Recovery needs, support and education may require coordination.

questions.rationale: Early planning supports safe transition and identifies home-care needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which discharge instruction is most important after surgery?

options.text: Warning signs such as fever, worsening pain, bleeding or breathing difficulty.

questions.rationale: Patients must know which symptoms require urgent review.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: A patient has a drain with suddenly increased bright-red output. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Sudden bright-red drainage may indicate bleeding.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which action best supports surgical-site infection prevention?

options.text: Aseptic wound care and hand hygiene.

questions.rationale: Aseptic technique and hand hygiene are central to infection prevention.

questions.sectionLabel: Surgical Nursing and Prevention of Complications
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe surgical nursing?

options.text: The patient receives pain medicine only.
The patient is prepared correctly, monitored closely, complications are prevented and discharge education is understood.

questions.rationale: Safe surgical nursing spans preparation, monitoring, prevention, recovery and education.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: An older patient is newly confused, febrile, hypoxic and passing less urine. What is the nurse's priority interpretation?
questions.rationale: New confusion with fever, hypoxia and reduced urine output suggests acute deterioration and possible sepsis, requiring urgent assessment and escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of an ABCDE assessment?

options.text: It organises urgent assessment while supporting clinical judgement.
It is used only in intensive care.
It applies only after medical review.

questions.rationale: ABCDE provides a structured approach to urgent assessment but does not replace professional judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure, diabetes and chronic kidney disease becomes breathless. What should the nurse do FIRST?

options.text: Assume heart failure is the cause.
Complete a focused assessment to identify possible cardiac, respiratory, fluid and metabolic causes.

questions.rationale: Comorbidity means breathlessness may have several causes; assessment should precede assumptions.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which patient should the nurse assess FIRST?

options.text: A stable patient awaiting discharge papers.
A patient requesting a meal change.
A patient with new chest pain and diaphoresis.

questions.rationale: New chest pain with diaphoresis may indicate acute cardiac ischaemia and requires immediate review.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient's respiratory rate has risen steadily over four hours while blood pressure remains normal. What is the BEST action?

options.text: Assess and escalate the trend promptly.

questions.rationale: A rising respiratory rate may be an early sign of deterioration despite normal blood pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: During handover, a patient is described as 'a little confused.' What should the receiving nurse do?

options.text: Establish baseline cognition and assess for acute causes.

questions.rationale: New confusion should be assessed as a possible acute change rather than attributed automatically to age.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which information belongs in the Assessment part of ISBAR?

options.text: The current clinical findings and interpretation.

questions.rationale: Assessment communicates current findings and the nurse's clinical interpretation.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A deteriorating patient's first escalation receives no timely response. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue through the approved escalation pathway.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue until the response matches the urgency of the patient's condition.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which finding is unexpected and therefore requires review?

options.text: Mild incisional pain improving with analgesia.
Reduced appetite on the first postoperative morning.

questions.rationale: Persistent tachycardia despite pain relief may indicate bleeding, infection, hypovolaemia or another complication.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: What is the most important principle when prioritising care for several patients?

options.text: Base priority on instability, acute change and risk.
Respond first to the longest request.

questions.rationale: Prioritisation should be based on urgency and risk, not convenience or routine.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient has a normal early warning score but looks acutely unwell. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use clinical judgement, reassess and escalate concern.

questions.rationale: Structured tools support but do not replace clinical judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which laboratory result is especially relevant when a patient with kidney disease receives multiple medicines?
questions.rationale: Renal impairment affects fluid balance, electrolytes and medication clearance.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes is fasting for surgery and becomes shaky and confused. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Fasting and diabetes treatment can cause hypoglycaemia, which requires immediate assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Why should a nurse compare current findings with baseline?

options.text: To identify new and clinically significant change.

questions.rationale: Baseline comparison helps distinguish chronic findings from acute deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient with COPD has worsening breathlessness and oedema. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Give a diuretic without an order.
Assess for both respiratory and cardiac causes.

questions.rationale: Combined cardiac and respiratory disease may produce overlapping symptoms, requiring comprehensive assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which handover statement is MOST effective?

options.text: 'Mr Khan has new confusion, RR 30, SpO2 88% on oxygen, reduced urine output and needs urgent review.'

questions.rationale: Risk-focused handover should communicate specific current findings and required action.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: A patient has several chronic conditions but develops sudden unilateral weakness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Treat as an acute neurological emergency and escalate.

questions.rationale: New unilateral weakness may indicate stroke and requires urgent action.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates structured prioritisation?

options.text: Addressing acute hypoxia before routine wound care.

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing concerns take priority over routine interventions.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Why is reduced urine output important in a deteriorating patient?

options.text: It is always expected in older adults.
It matters only after kidney surgery.
It may indicate reduced perfusion or renal compromise.

questions.rationale: Falling urine output can be an early sign of hypovolaemia, shock or renal dysfunction.

questions.sectionLabel: Advanced Assessment and Prioritisation in International Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective advanced assessment?

options.text: The nurse integrated trends, comorbidities and clinical judgement to act early.

questions.rationale: Effective assessment integrates structured tools with context and timely action.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A postoperative patient remains tachycardic despite pain relief and develops abdominal distension and low urine output. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recognise failure to progress and escalate for urgent review.

questions.rationale: Persistent tachycardia, distension and oliguria may indicate postoperative complications requiring urgent assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which factor increases perioperative risk?
questions.rationale: Frailty, anticoagulation, obesity, smoking and multiple comorbidities increase perioperative risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient with combined cardiac and respiratory disease becomes breathless. What is the best nursing approach?

options.text: Assume one diagnosis explains all symptoms.
Give oxygen without prescription or assessment.
Assess oxygenation, fluid status, circulation and treatment response.

questions.rationale: Breathlessness may be multifactorial and requires integrated assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: What does 'expected recovery trajectory' mean?

options.text: A fixed timetable identical for every patient.
The usual pattern of improvement after treatment or surgery.

questions.rationale: Expected trajectory helps nurses recognise when recovery is delayed or worsening.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests failure to progress after surgery?

options.text: Persistent tachycardia, poor intake and increasing abdominal distension.

questions.rationale: Persistent or worsening abnormalities may signal complications.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient with renal impairment receives a medicine cleared by the kidneys. What should the nurse consider?
questions.rationale: Renal impairment may reduce clearance and increase toxicity.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which postoperative finding requires urgent assessment?
questions.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling and pain may indicate venous thromboembolism.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes has unstable glucose during acute illness. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Continue the usual plan without reassessment.
Increase monitoring and coordinate treatment based on current risk.

questions.rationale: Acute illness and fasting can destabilise glucose, requiring individualised monitoring and treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient is breathless after surgery. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess airway, breathing, oxygen saturation, pain and possible complications.

questions.rationale: Postoperative breathlessness may reflect respiratory compromise, embolism, pain or fluid issues and requires assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Why should monitoring plans be individualised?

options.text: Risk varies with age, frailty, comorbidities, treatment and procedure.
Monitoring is determined only by bed location.

questions.rationale: Monitoring intensity should reflect the patient's specific risk factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure and kidney disease gains weight and becomes oedematous. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Fluid balance, respiratory status, renal results and treatment response.

questions.rationale: The findings suggest fluid overload requiring integrated cardiorenal assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which action best evaluates treatment effectiveness?

options.text: Ask whether the patient liked the treatment.
Compare current symptoms and observations with baseline and expected goals.

questions.rationale: Treatment evaluation requires reassessment against clinical goals.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A postoperative patient has persistent severe pain despite analgesia. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: Persistent pain may indicate a complication and requires further assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which intervention helps prevent perioperative respiratory complications?

options.text: Pain control, deep breathing and early mobilisation.

questions.rationale: These measures support ventilation and reduce atelectasis and pneumonia risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A frail patient cannot mobilise as expected after surgery. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess pain, strength, cognition and complications, and involve the multidisciplinary team.

questions.rationale: Failure to mobilise may reflect multiple barriers requiring assessment and coordinated care.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient on anticoagulants develops new bruising and hypotension. What is the priority?

options.text: Assess for bleeding and escalate urgently.

questions.rationale: Bruising with hypotension may indicate significant bleeding.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient has COPD and heart failure. Which fluid plan is safest?

options.text: One based on current fluid status, respiratory findings, renal function and orders.

questions.rationale: Fluid management must balance cardiac, respiratory and renal needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which finding suggests postoperative infection?

options.text: Increasing wound redness, pain and fever.

questions.rationale: Worsening wound inflammation with fever suggests infection.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: A patient is not eating after abdominal surgery and has delayed bowel function. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess for ileus or other complications and escalate persistent abnormalities.

questions.rationale: Poor intake and delayed bowel function may signal ileus or another complication.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Complex Medical and Perioperative Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects effective complex-care nursing?

options.text: The patient followed a standard pathway unchanged.
The nurse identified interacting risks, monitored response and adapted care promptly.

questions.rationale: Complex care requires integration of comorbidities, treatment effects and recovery patterns.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of multidisciplinary collaboration?

options.text: Coordinate care around the patient's goals and needs.
Allow one profession to lead every decision.

questions.rationale: Collaboration integrates expertise and clarifies responsibilities around patient goals.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which handover information is MOST important?

options.text: A list of routine tasks only.
Current condition, recent changes, risks, pending results and required actions.

questions.rationale: Risk-focused handover makes current concerns and actions visible.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which documentation entry is most appropriate?

options.text: 'Patient declined physiotherapy due to pain 8/10; analgesia given and review arranged.'

questions.rationale: Objective documentation describes findings, actions and follow-up without judgemental labels.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient is medically stable but cannot manage stairs at home. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask family to manage without review.
Coordinate functional assessment and support before discharge.

questions.rationale: Safe discharge depends on function and support, not medical stability alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which professional is most likely to assess home equipment needs?
questions.rationale: Occupational therapists assess function, activities and equipment needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: What should be included in discharge planning for a wound-care patient?

options.text: Wound instructions, supplies, follow-up, warning signs and support.

questions.rationale: Safe transition requires practical care instructions and clear escalation advice.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient has a pending test result at discharge. What is essential?

options.text: Assume the patient will follow up.
Ignore it if the patient feels well.
Clear responsibility for review and communication of the result.

questions.rationale: Pending results require defined ownership to prevent missed follow-up.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which statement best describes medication reconciliation at transition?

options.text: Comparing the patient's actual medicines with current orders and resolving differences.

questions.rationale: Reconciliation reduces omissions, duplication and confusion during transitions.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient requires physiotherapy, dietetic and social-work input. What should guide coordination?

options.text: The patient's clinical priorities, goals and discharge needs.
The order in which staff are available.

questions.rationale: Coordination should be patient-centred and risk-focused.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which handover statement is inadequate?

options.text: 'Patient has new oxygen requirement and needs review.'

questions.rationale: Vague language such as 'fine' does not convey clinical risk or current needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Why should documentation include the patient's response to intervention?

options.text: It is required only for legal reasons.
It shows whether the intervention was effective and guides further care.

questions.rationale: Response data support evaluation and continuity.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A transfer form omits the patient's falls risk. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the receiving team will assess later.
Clarify and communicate the risk before transfer.

questions.rationale: Current risks must be communicated during transfer to prevent harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient lives alone and has limited transport for follow-up. What is the BEST nursing action?

options.text: Assess barriers and coordinate community or social support.
Tell the patient to solve it.

questions.rationale: Social circumstances affect safe continuity of care and should be addressed.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which documentation best supports legal accountability?

options.text: A brief note written days later.
Timely, objective records of findings, reasoning, actions, escalation and response.

questions.rationale: Accurate contemporaneous documentation supports communication and accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: During handover, a nurse lists tasks but omits why they matter. What is the risk?

options.text: The receiving nurse may not understand priorities or urgency.

questions.rationale: Clinical meaning is needed to prioritise and act safely.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient is discharged with new mobility equipment. What should occur before leaving?

options.text: Ask family to read the manual.
Confirm correct use through demonstration and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Safe use should be confirmed before discharge.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which action best prevents fragmentation of care?

options.text: Clarify roles, share relevant information and document the agreed plan.
Allow each discipline to work independently.

questions.rationale: Clear responsibilities and shared plans promote coordinated care.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: A patient refuses a proposed discharge plan. What should the team do?

options.text: Explore concerns, discuss options and involve the patient in decisions.

questions.rationale: Shared decision-making respects autonomy and may reveal practical barriers.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: What is the nurse's key role in transitions of care?

options.text: Transfer all responsibility to the patient.
Coordinate information, risks, treatment and support across settings.

questions.rationale: Nurses help ensure continuity across professionals and settings.

questions.sectionLabel: Interdisciplinary Care, Documentation and Safe Transitions
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects a safe transition?

options.text: The patient and receiving team understand the plan, risks, follow-up and responsibilities.

questions.rationale: Safe transitions depend on shared understanding and clear responsibility.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: What is the first step in planning patient education?

options.text: Assess learning needs, health literacy and barriers.

questions.rationale: Education should be based on individual needs, abilities and circumstances.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which statement best describes teach-back?

options.text: The patient explains the plan in their own words or demonstrates a skill.

questions.rationale: Teach-back checks whether the explanation was effective.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient with COPD cannot distinguish a preventer inhaler from a reliever. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use clear visual cues, demonstration and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Practical, accessible education can correct misunderstanding and improve self-management.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which factor may reduce treatment adherence?

options.text: Cost, side effects, misunderstanding or cultural beliefs.

questions.rationale: Adherence barriers are often practical or informational and should be assessed before judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient with heart failure should be taught to report:

options.text: Rapid weight gain and worsening breathlessness.

questions.rationale: These may indicate fluid overload and deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient has low health literacy. Which teaching method is BEST?

options.text: Plain language, visual aids, small steps and teach-back.

questions.rationale: Accessible, structured teaching improves understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient cannot afford prescribed dietary changes. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore realistic alternatives and involve appropriate support.

questions.rationale: Self-management plans should be realistic and adapted to resources.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which action best supports shared decision-making?

options.text: Explain options, benefits and risks and invite patient preferences.

questions.rationale: Shared decisions promote informed participation and trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient with diabetes can describe symptoms of hypoglycaemia but not what to do. What is missing?

options.text: An action plan for treatment and seeking help.

questions.rationale: Education should include recognition and clear response steps.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which self-monitoring instruction is appropriate for heart failure?

options.text: Record daily weight under similar conditions and know the escalation threshold.

questions.rationale: Consistent daily monitoring supports early detection of fluid retention.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient nods during education but cannot explain the plan. What should the nurse conclude?

options.text: Understanding has not been confirmed and teaching should be adapted.

questions.rationale: Passive agreement is not evidence of understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: How should education be adapted for a patient with hearing impairment?

options.text: Face the patient, reduce background noise, use written support and confirm understanding.

questions.rationale: Communication should be accessible and respectful.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient wants to continue a cultural dietary practice that conflicts with the care plan. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore the practice respectfully and negotiate safe alternatives.

questions.rationale: Culturally responsive care seeks safe, realistic solutions without assumptions.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of self-management education?

options.text: Transfer all responsibility to the patient.
Build the patient's confidence to manage treatment and recognise deterioration.

questions.rationale: Self-management education supports informed daily decisions and early help-seeking.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient frequently misses follow-up because transport is unavailable. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Identify the barrier and coordinate suitable support or alternatives.

questions.rationale: Practical barriers should be addressed to support continuity.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which discharge statement requires correction?

options.text: 'I will seek help if breathlessness worsens.'
'I will stop my medicine once I feel better.'

questions.rationale: Stopping medicine without advice may lead to deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient demonstrates inhaler technique incorrectly after teaching. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Re-teach, allow practice and reassess technique.

questions.rationale: Skills should be demonstrated correctly before discharge.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which education plan is most person-centred?

options.text: One aligned with the patient's goals, language, culture, finances and daily routine.
A plan based only on diagnosis.

questions.rationale: Person-centred education is tailored to the individual's circumstances.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: A patient with several chronic conditions receives conflicting advice from different clinicians. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Coordinate clarification and provide one consistent plan.

questions.rationale: Conflicting advice undermines safety and should be reconciled through the team.

questions.sectionLabel: Person-Centred Education and Chronic Disease Self-Management
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective self-management education?

options.text: The patient can explain the plan, demonstrate key skills and identify when to seek help.

questions.rationale: Understanding and practical capability are the meaningful outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates clinical leadership in adult medical-surgical nursing?

options.text: Remaining visible, supporting complex decisions and maintaining standards during workload pressure.
Completing administrative work away from the ward.
Allowing standards to vary during busy periods.
Taking over all difficult patients personally.

questions.rationale: Clinical leaders remain accessible, support judgement and protect care standards even when workload is high.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A junior nurse is worried about a patient whose early warning score has not reached the trigger threshold. What is the BEST leadership response?

options.text: Tell the nurse to wait for the score to rise.
Review the patient and support escalation based on clinical concern.
Ask the nurse to document only.
Dismiss the concern because the score is normal.

questions.rationale: Scoring tools support but do not replace professional judgement. Leaders should reinforce escalation based on genuine clinical concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which feature most strongly reflects psychological safety?

options.text: Staff avoid questions to protect confidence.
Only senior nurses may challenge decisions.
Staff can admit uncertainty and raise concerns without humiliation.
Errors are discussed only privately by managers.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety enables early communication and learning while preserving accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A unit has repeated variation in postoperative assessment quality. What should the nurse leader do FIRST?

options.text: Review current practice and identify gaps in assessment, competence and workflow.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins with understanding actual practice and contributing factors before choosing interventions.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which mentoring strategy best develops clinical reasoning?

options.text: Use case review, guided questioning and reflective feedback.

questions.rationale: Case-based coaching helps nurses connect assessment cues, priorities and action.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse repeatedly misses subtle deterioration despite completing all observation charts. What is the BEST development approach?

options.text: Focus on trend interpretation and clinical reasoning through supervised case review.
Reduce the nurse's patient contact permanently.

questions.rationale: The gap is not task completion but interpretation; targeted coaching and supervised practice are appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: What should a leader do when efficiency targets begin to reduce dignity and communication?

options.text: Rebalance workflow so standards remain person-centred.

questions.rationale: Efficiency should not override dignity, choice or communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates effective leadership presence?

options.text: Staff seek help early and complex patients receive timely review.

questions.rationale: Visible, supportive leadership promotes early escalation and safer care.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A senior nurse publicly criticises a junior nurse for escalating a concern that proved non-urgent. What should the leader do?

options.text: Address the behaviour and reinforce that appropriate escalation is supported.
Ignore it because no harm occurred.
Ask the junior nurse to apologise.

questions.rationale: Humiliation undermines psychological safety and may delay future escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects accountability within psychological safety?

options.text: No one is accountable for errors.
Staff can speak up, but unsafe behaviour is still reviewed fairly.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety and accountability are complementary, not opposing principles.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A leader wants to strengthen assessment reliability. Which strategy is MOST effective?

options.text: Standardise key expectations, observe practice, provide feedback and audit outcomes.

questions.rationale: Reliable practice requires clear standards, coaching and monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which behaviour best models person-centred professional practice?

options.text: Avoiding family involvement even when requested.
Including patient goals in care decisions while maintaining safety.

questions.rationale: Person-centred leadership protects individual needs within safe care systems.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A team is reluctant to question a dominant surgeon. What is the leader's priority?

options.text: Create explicit escalation expectations and support respectful challenge regardless of hierarchy.
Tell staff to follow senior decisions.

questions.rationale: Hierarchy should not prevent staff from raising safety concerns.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse makes an appropriate but unsuccessful escalation attempt. What should the leader encourage next?

options.text: Continue through the approved escalation pathway until the response matches urgency.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue when the response is inadequate for the patient's condition.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which indicator best reflects staff competence in adult acute care?

options.text: Observed assessment quality, reasoning, escalation and patient outcomes.

questions.rationale: Competence is demonstrated through performance and outcomes, not merely participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A leader introduces simulation for deterioration scenarios. What is the MAIN purpose?

options.text: Build recognition, communication and team response in a safe environment.

questions.rationale: Simulation supports practice of assessment, prioritisation and escalation without patient risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which action most strongly protects care standards during high workload?

options.text: Adjust staffing and priorities while preserving essential assessment and escalation.
Allow safety checks to be shortened.

questions.rationale: Leadership should adapt workload and resources without compromising critical care standards.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: A patient complains that staff discuss tasks but rarely explain care. What should the leader do?

options.text: Review communication practice and reinforce patient involvement in care pathways.

questions.rationale: Person-centred care requires explanation, involvement and respectful communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates a mature clinical leadership culture?

options.text: Incidents are rare because they are unreported.
Staff speak up early, receive fair support and consistently use evidence-based care.

questions.rationale: A mature culture combines openness, competence, consistency and learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Excellence in Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing
questions.stem: What is the overarching role of a Global Nursing Professional in adult care leadership?

options.text: Delegate all quality work to managers.
Connect bedside practice, workforce development and organisational improvement.

questions.rationale: Global Nursing Professionals influence both direct care and the systems that support it.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which statement best describes an effective deterioration-recognition system?

options.text: It combines reliable observations, trend recognition, clear triggers and timely response.
It relies only on one score.
It activates only after severe collapse.

questions.rationale: Effective systems combine measurement, judgement, escalation and response.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A hospital records observations consistently but still has delayed ICU transfers. What should leaders examine?

options.text: Response times, trend recognition and escalation barriers.

questions.rationale: Completion alone is insufficient; leaders must evaluate whether data lead to timely action.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which barrier most commonly delays escalation?
questions.rationale: Hierarchy and fear can suppress early concern and delay review.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A review shows rising respiratory rates were repeatedly normalised. What does this indicate?
questions.rationale: Repeated acceptance of abnormal findings as normal is a system risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which measure best evaluates a rapid-response system?

options.text: Time from trigger to clinical review.

questions.rationale: Response time directly reflects system performance after deterioration is recognised.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Why should family concerns be included in escalation systems?

options.text: Families may recognise subtle change before objective triggers are reached.

questions.rationale: Family observations can provide valuable early warning and should be assessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A nurse's escalation is dismissed because the patient 'always looks like that.' What system weakness is most evident?

options.text: Normalisation of abnormal findings and poor escalation culture.

questions.rationale: Familiarity can lead teams to overlook meaningful deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which review approach best supports learning after missed deterioration?

options.text: Focus only on the last nurse involved.
Use discipline as the first response.
Examine assessment, trends, communication, staffing, workload and system design.

questions.rationale: Missed deterioration is often multifactorial and requires systems analysis.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A hospital adds a direct nurse-concern escalation pathway. What problem is it designed to address?

options.text: Scores that may not capture all clinical risk.

questions.rationale: Clinical concern should be able to trigger review even without threshold scores.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which outcome indicates an escalation system is psychologically safe?

options.text: Staff activate it without fear of ridicule when genuinely concerned.
All activations lead to punishment if non-urgent.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety encourages timely activation based on concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A unit has delayed escalation during night shifts. Which action is BEST?

options.text: Analyse staffing, workload, access to review and communication patterns at night.

questions.rationale: Night-shift delays may reflect structural factors requiring targeted analysis and redesign.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which finding should trigger immediate review even if the total score is low?
questions.rationale: Acute neurological change may represent serious deterioration regardless of composite score.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A rapid-response team arrives, but team roles are unclear. What should leaders improve?

options.text: Defined activation roles and communication responsibilities.

questions.rationale: Clear roles improve coordinated response during urgent events.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: What is the primary value of trend-focused handover?

options.text: It highlights direction of change rather than isolated values.
It removes the need for assessment.

questions.rationale: Trends help teams detect deterioration earlier.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A patient deteriorates despite repeated escalation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue through the approved escalation chain while providing ongoing care.

questions.rationale: Escalation should continue until the response matches clinical urgency.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which process measure is most useful for deterioration systems?

options.text: Percentage of triggered observations followed by timely escalation.

questions.rationale: This directly measures whether the required response process occurred.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: A case review finds observations were entered late into the electronic record. Why is this important?

options.text: Delayed data visibility can delay trend recognition and escalation.

questions.rationale: Timely documentation is essential for shared recognition of deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which intervention is most likely to reduce delayed recognition?

options.text: Simulation, trend-focused handover and direct escalation pathways.

questions.rationale: Multimodal interventions address skill, communication and system access.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: What should leaders measure beyond observation completion?

options.text: Accuracy, trend recognition, escalation and response time.

questions.rationale: System performance depends on what happens after observations are recorded.

questions.sectionLabel: Systems for Recognising and Responding to Deterioration
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates a reliable deterioration system?

options.text: Subtle decline is recognised, escalated and treated before severe harm.

questions.rationale: Reliability is shown by timely recognition and response, not merely documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: What is the first step in an adult-care quality-improvement initiative?

options.text: Define a specific problem using baseline data.

questions.rationale: Improvement begins with a clearly defined problem and understanding current performance.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which is an outcome measure for postoperative pulmonary complications?
questions.rationale: Outcome measures describe what happened to patients.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which is a process measure?

options.text: Percentage of eligible patients mobilised within the target time.

questions.rationale: Process measures show whether recommended care occurred.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Why are balancing measures important?

options.text: They identify unintended effects such as increased pain or workload.

questions.rationale: Balancing measures ensure improvements do not create new problems.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A ward introduces early mobilisation but pain scores rise. What should the team do?

options.text: Review pain management and adapt the pathway.

questions.rationale: The intervention should be refined using balancing data.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which strategy best translates evidence into practice?

options.text: Convert guidelines into practical tools, education, equipment and workflow.

questions.rationale: Evidence translation requires integration into everyday work.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Why are small tests of change useful?

options.text: They allow learning and adaptation before wider implementation.

questions.rationale: Small tests reduce risk and improve local fit.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A unit has high pressure-injury rates. What should leaders do before selecting an intervention?

options.text: Map current practice and analyse contributing factors.

questions.rationale: Understanding the current process helps target the real causes.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which measure best evaluates sustained improvement?
questions.rationale: Sustainability requires continued measurement over time.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Patient experience should be included because:

options.text: It is the only outcome that matters.
Quality includes both clinical outcomes and how care is experienced.
It applies only to outpatient care.

questions.rationale: High-quality care includes safety, effectiveness and patient experience.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A falls project reduces falls but increases use of restrictive measures. What should the team conclude?

options.text: A balancing harm may have been introduced.

questions.rationale: Reducing one outcome should not create new harm or loss of function.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which action best supports evidence translation by nurse leaders?

options.text: Engage frontline staff and adapt evidence to local workflow.

questions.rationale: Local adaptation and staff involvement improve implementation.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A surgical pathway is followed inconsistently. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Audit the process and identify where and why reliability breaks down.

questions.rationale: Process audit reveals implementation gaps and barriers.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which statement best describes a PDSA approach?

options.text: Plan a change, test it, study results and adapt.

questions.rationale: PDSA supports iterative learning and refinement.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A project improves clinical outcomes but substantially increases staff workload. What should leaders do?

options.text: Review workflow and balancing measures before wider spread.

questions.rationale: Implementation must be effective and sustainable.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which data source may help identify readmission priorities?

options.text: Readmission trends combined with patient and process data.

questions.rationale: Multiple relevant data sources help define patterns and causes.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Why is process mapping useful?

options.text: It shows how care is actually delivered and where failures occur.

questions.rationale: Process mapping makes workflow and failure points visible.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which intervention is most likely to sustain a new evidence-based practice?

options.text: Embed it in workflow, training, equipment, audit and feedback.

questions.rationale: Sustainability requires integration and ongoing feedback.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: A team improves mobilisation rates but readmissions remain unchanged. What should they do?

options.text: Review whether mobilisation addressed the main causes of readmission.

questions.rationale: Improved process does not guarantee the intended outcome; causal assumptions should be reassessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Quality Improvement and Evidence Translation in Adult Care
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates successful evidence translation?

options.text: A practical pathway is used reliably and improves outcomes without unacceptable unintended effects.

questions.rationale: Success requires reliable practice change and measurable benefit.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Health, Integrated Care and Global Adult-Health Practice
questions.stem: What is the main benefit of electronic records in adult care?

options.text: Improved access to trends and shared care plans.

questions.rationale: Electronic records can improve access and coordination but still require verification.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Health, Integrated Care and Global Adult-Health Practice
questions.stem: Which digital risk can create false confidence?
questions.rationale: Poor-quality data may appear authoritative and mislead clinicians.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Health, Integrated Care and Global Adult-Health Practice
questions.stem: What is automation bias?

options.text: Over-reliance on technology despite conflicting clinical evidence.

questions.rationale: Automation bias occurs when users trust a system more than their own assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Health, Integrated Care and Global Adult-Health Practice
questions.stem: A predictive tool labels a patient low risk, but the nurse sees deterioration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for the score to change.
Use clinical judgement and escalate based on the full assessment.

questions.rationale: Technology supports but does not replace professional judgement.

questions.sectionLabel: Digital Health, Integrated Care and Global Adult-Health Practice
